extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians and comedy performers learning or improving live crowd work
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for performing crowd work (audience improvisation) during live stand-up shows, focusing on listening, safety, building jokes from audience offers, and integrating crowd work with written material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen and find a specific detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedian listens to audience members and locates an unusual, specific detail to work from rather than relying on generic prompts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't ask generic questions; find the unusual detail and pull at the thread. The page contrasts this with repetitive setups and emphasizes active listening rather than waiting to speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the audience member with care / don't punch down
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the volunteer feels safe — tease but do not humiliate or bully the person on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audience member must feel safe. Tease, don't humiliate. If the interaction feels mean, the audience may switch sides. Avoid bullying (listed as a pitfall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Build the joke on what was offered
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the volunteer's words or setup as the basis of the joke rather than forcing an unrelated bit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience members often say funny things — acknowledge it and build on their setup. 'Did the joke build on what was offered?' is an explicit rubric question. Also: work with whatever the volunteer offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to written material gracefully
rubrics_metrics.description: After a crowd-work moment, transition back into your prepared material without losing momentum or cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting crowd work become a permanent substitute for written material. 'Did the comedian return to written material gracefully?' is an explicit evaluation point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the moment feel singular (avoid genericity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd work moments should feel specific and unique to that show and person, not generic lines that could be used anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for unrepeatable moments; avoid repetitive, generic setups like 'what do you do?'. The rubric asks whether the moment felt singular (not generic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Build callbacks / stitch the show together
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference earlier audience interactions later in the show to create cohesion and recurring laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use callbacks to stitch the show together; reference earlier audience interactions so crowd work becomes part of the show's throughline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comfort with small talk
rubrics_metrics.description: The performer is comfortable initiating and sustaining casual conversational interactions required to coax usable material from audience members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a required skill; being at ease with small talk helps surface specifics and keep flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active listening (not waiting to speak)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedian listens attentively to what the volunteer is actually saying instead of focusing on planned retorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly listed: active listening helps catch workable details and build genuine interactions rather than preplanned zingers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letting go of ego
rubrics_metrics.description: The performer prioritizes the interaction and material over proving they are funniest, allowing the exchange to develop organically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a required skill: letting go of ego enables building on audience offers and acknowledging when the volunteer is the funnier source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with whatever the volunteer offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt to the volunteer's energy, facts, and jokes rather than forcing a particular angle or punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly listed; includes being flexible and harnessing whatever details the volunteer supplies, even if unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch workable details quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedian rapidly identifies elements of the interaction that can be turned into jokes or callbacks before the moment passes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed is important in live crowd work; this skill is called out as necessary to pull threads and create payoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create conversational flow
rubrics_metrics.description: The interaction should feel like a natural conversation with beats and callbacks, not a staccato Q&A or interrogation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a skill: creating flow keeps the room engaged and prevents the interaction from stalling or going long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid becoming a substitute for written material
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd work should complement, not replace, the comedian's prepared set; over-reliance on crowd work can be a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a pitfall: don't let crowd work become the main content of the set; it can erode the structure and branding of your material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetitive setups
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on the same generic prompts (e.g., 'what do you do?') that produce predictable, unoriginal interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetitive setups are flagged as a pitfall; instead, ask non-generic, specific questions and look for unusual details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bullying
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not humiliate or belittle volunteers as a source of laughs; bullying is both unethical and alienates the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a pitfall and tied to 'don't punch down.' If the audience perceives mean-spiritedness, they may turn on the comedian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting interactions run too long (don't lose the room)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep crowd work moments appropriately paced; overly long exchanges risk losing audience attention and momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a pitfall: long interactions can derail the show — know when to cut off or transition back to prepared material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimacy (connect on a personal level)
rubrics_metrics.description: One goal of crowd work is to create intimacy with the audience by engaging them personally and making the show feel direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed under 'Why Comedians Do It' — intimacy increases engagement and investment from the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unrepeatability / uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful crowd work yields moments that are one-off and specific to that performance and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being unrepeatable makes moments feel special and prevents 'burning' material; the rubric explicitly asks whether the moment felt singular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability (clips safe to post)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd work that produces memorable, self-contained moments can be clipped and posted online without 'burning' your written jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a reason comedians do crowd work: shareable moments extend reach while preserving scripted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showcase improvisation skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd work can demonstrate a comedian's improvisational sharpness and quick thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a benefit: performing strong crowd work signals a comedian's ability to think on their feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set saver (rescue failing material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use crowd work as a tool to recover when written material isn't landing, without letting it become a crutch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a reason to do crowd work; balance is important so it remains an occasional tool rather than the core set.
